CausalChain: Tumor glycolytic reprogramming -> Increased lactic acid production -> Lactic acid accumulation in tumor microenvironment -> Uptake of lactic acid by MDSCs -> Epigenetic modulation of MDSC gene expression -> Upregulation of ARG1, iNOS, COX-2 -> Enhanced MDSC suppressive activity -> Inhibition of T-cell mediated anti-tumor responses -> Tumor immune evasion
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived lactic acid acts as an epigenetic modulator that reprograms MDSCs to acquire a heightened immunosuppressive phenotype; therefore, blocking lactate transport in the tumor microenvironment will normalize MDSC differentiation and enhance the efficacy of checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy.
Abstract: Recent evidence underscores the significance of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in mediating tumor immune evasion across a spectrum of cancers. Here, we propose that tumor metabolic reprogramming, notably through enhanced glycolysis, results in lactic acid accumulation that acts as an epigenetic modulator of MDSC differentiation and suppressive function. Specifically, we hypothesize that the influx of lactic acid into MDSCs drives upregulation of immunosuppressive mediators including arginase 1, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and COX‐2, which collectively impair effector T cell responses. Consequently, pharmacological inhibition of lactate transporters (e.g., MCT1/MCT4) may reduce lactic acid levels in the tumor microenvironment, restore normal myeloid differentiation, and enhance responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors. This integrated approach, combining metabolic modulation with immunotherapy, offers a promising strategy to overcome the resistance associated with MDSC‐mediated immune suppression.
